title: Unequal Coherent Ergotropy at Equal Interferometric Visibility and Energy in Quantum-Controlled Interferometers
authors: Tonipe Anuradha, André H. A. Malavazi, Borhan Ahmadi, Lucas Pollyceno, Pedro R. Dieguez
abstract: The ergotropy, or unitarily extractable work, of a quantum system naturally splits into incoherent and coherent contributions, respectively set by population inversion and coherences in the energy eigenbasis. We show that this split makes the coherent ergotropy of a Mach--Zehnder qubit sensitive to path predictability that the output interference fringes do not reveal. We send the path qubit, prepared as a thermal quantum battery, through two quantum-controlled interferometers built from the same elements, a fixed beam splitter and a beam splitter coherently controlled to be present or absent, differing only in the order in which these two act. The two arrangements share identical visibility, stored energy, and incoherent ergotropy at every point in the parameter space. Yet, for work extracted from the output battery alone, placing the controlled beam splitter first never yields less coherent ergotropy, and at fixed visibility and interferometric phase the difference is governed by the path predictability that this ordering creates. The same expression reappears as a purity deficit on the beam-splitter controller, so the work advantage comes with a Landauer bound on the cost of locally resetting the controller that is never larger at the same temperature. We further examine the effects of decoherence on the battery and consider a relativistic realization in which a Wigner rotation correlates the particle's spin with its path. Tracing out the spin decoheres the battery and allows the two arrangements to exhibit different coherent ergotropies even in regimes where their non-relativistic counterparts coincide. These results show that interference visibility is not a complete measure of the coherence available as work.
summary: This paper analyzes quantum interferometers to show that the extractable work (ergotropy) is not fully characterized by interference visibility. By comparing two experimental setups, the authors demonstrate that the path predictability retained by the setup—a resource inaccessible to simple output measurements—contributes a measurable, non-zero amount to the coherent work. This establishes path information as a distinct, operational thermodynamic resource.
main_problem: The study investigates whether the coherent ergotropy (unitarily extractable work) in quantum interferometers is solely determined by output visibility or if it is sensitive to path predictability inaccessible to standard measurements.
main_result: The coherent ergotropy differs between two interferometer setups (QDCE vs. QCRE), showing that path predictability retained by the setup acts as an additional, measurable thermodynamic resource beyond what is revealed by interference visibility.
method: The authors compare the coherent ergotropy extracted from the output battery for two specific Mach-Zehnder interferometer arrangements, analyzing the difference using path predictability and Landauer-bound related costs.
model_or_system: The system is a Mach-Zehnder interferometer (MZI) using a two-level system (TLS) as both a quantum battery and a which-path probe. The analysis compares two protocols: the Quantum Delayed-Choice Experiment (QDCE) and the Quantum-Controlled Reality Experiment (QCRE).

paper_structure: The paper establishes the theoretical framework by defining ergotropy and comparing the QDCE and QCRE protocols. It derives the observables for both setups, analyzes the difference in coherent ergotropy, and extends the findings to a relativistic realization involving spin-path correlation.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, measurable example where standard quantum coherence measures (like visibility) fail to capture the full thermodynamic resource content, linking quantum foundations (which-path information) directly to thermodynamics (extractable work).
